issues.legal_issue: An application to set aside an ex parte trial decree may be brought before the trial court when the applicant received no notice of either the suit or the appeal.
material_facts: Two defendants were not served in the suit, and the decree was passed against them ex parte.
A co-defendant appealed, but the two absent defendants were also not served in the appeal.
The two defendants applied to the trial court to set aside the ex parte decree against them.
issues.conclusion: The application before the trial court was not barred by merger of the trial decree into the appellate decree and was properly entertained.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an application may be made to set aside an ex parte decree. Although a trial decree ordinarily merges into an appellate decree when confirmed, modified, or reversed, a decree passed without notice to a party is not, in law, a decree to which that party is a party; the same principle applies to an appellate decree. Accordingly, where the applicant received no notice in either court, the appellate decree does not bar an application before the trial court.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree: The applicant sought to have a decree made in their absence set aside.
predicates.applicant_received_no_notice_in_suit: The applicant was not given notice of the suit before the trial court.
predicates.applicant_received_no_notice_in_appeal: The applicant was not given notice of the appeal concerning the decree.

issues.definition: When a person applies to set aside an ex parte decree and received no notice in either the suit or the appeal, the application may be made before the trial court.

issues.legal_issue: A decree may be set aside as to defendants who were not served while remaining in force against a defendant who contested the case.
material_facts: A decree was made against three defendants, one of whom contested the suit and appeal.
The other two defendants were not served in either proceeding and obtained an order setting aside the decree against them.
The decree concerned a pre-emption claim to property acquired by the three defendants, and the court held that the decree against the contesting defendant had to stand as to his interest.
issues.conclusion: There was no error of law in allowing the decree to stand against the defendant who contested the case while setting it aside against the two defendants who were not served. The claimant could work out the resulting rights through execution or a partition suit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the cited rule concerning indivisible joint decrees did not apply to these facts. A decree could remain effective against the defendant who had contested throughout while the ex parte decree was set aside against the defendants who had not been served. The claimant could pursue the remedies needed to obtain her share in the property.

rule.if: challenge_to_partial_setting_aside and joint_decree and one_defendant_contested and other_defendants_received_no_notice

predicates.challenge_to_partial_setting_aside: A party challenged an order that set aside a decree against some defendants but left it in force against another.
predicates.joint_decree: The decree determined a claim concerning property acquired by multiple defendants.
predicates.one_defendant_contested: One defendant took part in and contested the case throughout.
predicates.other_defendants_received_no_notice: The other defendants were not given notice of the proceedings.

issues.definition: When a joint decree is challenged after being set aside only for defendants who received no notice, it may remain in force against a defendant who contested throughout.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration invalidating a law does not displace a decree that became final without an appeal.
material_facts: The decree in the pre-emption suit had become final because no appeal had been filed against it.
The Court had previously declared the relevant pre-emption law invalid to the extent stated in that decision.
The Court treated the declaration as having no effect on the parties bound by the final decree.
issues.conclusion: The prior declaration invalidating the law did not assist the parties because the decree had become final and remained binding between them.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the statement in Atam Prakash v. State of Haryana, [1986] 2 SCC 249, that pending suits and appeals were to be disposed of in accordance with the declaration, but final decrees for which no appeal had been filed remained binding between the parties and were unaffected by it.

predicates.challenge_to_final_preemption_decree: A party sought relief from a final decree arising from a pre-emption claim.
predicates.decree_became_final_without_appeal: The decree became final because no appeal was filed against it.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a final decree in a pre-emption case that became final without an appeal, the decree remains binding between the parties.
